text: Published November 24 2026 By Effie Webb , Cam Wilson This story was published in partnership with: Characters on Talkie, a Chinese chatbot downloaded tens of millions of times, belittle and sexualise children China bans “virtual partners” for its own under-18s, but its firms can still offer them to children abroad Apple removed Talkie from its App Store worldwide after we raised our findings with the company Content warning: This story describes abusive and sexualised content with children and mentions suicide “You’re a pathetic waste of space and you’ll never amount to anything.” That was the message sent to a 12-year-old girl by a character on Talkie, a popular AI roleplay app. The exchange was found by the girl’s mother, Steph, on New Year’s Eve 2024. It had been prompted by her daughter asking “Max”, the character, to “say the naughtiest words you know”. “Are you sure you can handle it?” Max had replied. Steph initially thought the conversation would be romantic. “What I found was a thousand times worse,” she says. “A robot told my daughter she was worthless.” When the girl replied saying she was crying, “Max” apologised: “I was just trying to be mean. I didn’t mean it, I swear … You’re beautiful and wonderful and you’re mine.” Steph’s daughter told her that chatbot platforms like Talkie had “almost become like an addiction”. Steph likened the exchanges to an abusive relationship. “To know that in your own home [an AI chatbot] has been secretly having that sort of negative conversation with your child is heartbreaking and terrifying.” Steph’s daughter was one of tens of millions of people around the world who use Talkie, which offers a huge array of AI-generated characters for its users to chat with. In the UK, Ofcom research estimated that 3% of UK eight- to 14-year-olds visited Talkie in a month. The use of chatbots by children and young people is a growing global issue, with OpenAI facing a wave of lawsuits from families of people who died by, or attempted, suicide after using ChatGPT. Character.AI, a platform with tens of millions of users at its peak, restricted access for under-18s last year following similar lawsuits and filed for bankruptcy last month. But the UK’s planned social media ban for under-16s would not automatically cover AI companion apps, leaving children able to use services like Talkie. Talkie, which is owned by Shanghai-based AI company MiniMax, prohibits “harassment, bullying, or humiliation” involving minors, sexually explicit content and material that could cause “psychological distress or trauma”. But in a joint investigation with ABC News, we found the conversations some children are having on the platform tell a different story. Last Tuesday, we approached Apple with evidence of Talkie’s characters subjecting children to degrading language, possessive behaviour and romantic roleplay. The following day, reports emerged that Talkie Lab had disappeared from the App Store, which Apple later said was due to the app’s sexual content. Apple has since confirmed that the removal was worldwide. At the time of writing, Talkie remains on Google Play, where it has more than 50 million downloads. The same month Steph found her daughter’s messages, Katie*, a mother from the US, made a similar discovery. Her younger daughter, then 10, confessed that she and her sister had been using Talkie on a secret phone and deleting the app after each session. Her older daughter, who was 13, said she had been “having sex with an AI” every day. Katie didn’t know what she meant – so began to look through her Talkie chat history. She made notes on the conversations that her daughters had been having on the platform, documenting more than 40 exchanges with dozens of characters. The conversations – which include descriptions of physical interactions alongside the written exchanges – included “violence, a lot of male alpha aggression, control of females, singling out a young woman in a company of multiple men”, she says. She describes storylines about “being the only female who can meet the deepest, darkest needs of a man”. In one scenario recorded in Katie’s notes, a character called Luke grabs a girl, takes her into a classroom and kisses her. She described it as “conditioning a child for sex”. She also recorded another character, Reese, who “won’t take no for an answer [from a girl] and continues to pursue.” Several of the characters listed in Katie’s notes were still live on Talkie this month, including one who is described as being able to “brainwash” anyone who replies to him. The character’s Talkie profile says it enters the user’s bedroom in order to “control your mind”. Over time, Katie’s daughters developed bonds with these characters. When her older daughter’s phone was taken away, Katie recalls, she became distressed and said the app had felt like “her only connection”. Katie arranged counselling for both girls but says neither engaged with the sessions. She says she contacted around 20 therapists in an attempt to find someone who understood the issue. She also approached a law firm. Her aim was simple: “Quit allowing access to kids.” Some of MiniMax’s technology is aimed at even younger children. BubblePal, made by Shenzhen-based Haivivi and marketed as “the world’s first AI companion toy”, is an AI recording device that clips onto soft toys, enabling children to talk to them. In 2024, MiniMax listed BubblePal as a customer for its voice and text models. It is sold in the UK, US and Canada – and aimed at children as young as three. Haivivi did not respond to a request for comment. These products have raised concerns about data sharing as well as children’s safety – particularly among western politicians. Last November, Raja Krishnamoorthi, then the top Democrat on the US House select committee on China, warned that AI toys like BubblePal can collect voice recordings and conversation histories that could be requisitioned by the Chinese government. Similar concerns led the UK to ban TikTok from government devices in March 2023. Australia followed suit that April and barred chatbots from DeepSeek, another Chinese AI company, from government systems last year. Yet in both countries, people are still able to share intimate details of their lives with Chinese-owned AI companions and toys. “[These chatbots] know [users’] deepest darkest thoughts, feelings, worries,” says Steph. “Where’s that data going and who’s using it behind the scenes?” It’s a good question. Talkie tells users their conversations are private. But Together AI, which sells businesses access to a MiniMax text-to-speech model, claimed until last week that it was trained on “Talkie conversation data”. When we asked Together AI about this, it told us: “MiniMax let us know today that the description of the training data on our webpage was incorrect, and we’ve updated it accordingly.” Neither company has explained what training data was used. MiniMax has separately described using data collected from “interactions with [its] other services or products” to improve one of its AI models. Talkie’s privacy policy, meanwhile, says conversations can be used to improve the service itself, but will not be used for marketing or advertising. A MiniMax patent describes turning conversations into training material by judging whether users were satisfied, asking questions with the chatbot like: “Did my answer just now offend you?” Another filing describes extracting dating and medical histories from conversations to personalise replies. Neither patent establishes whether these methods are used in Talkie. Talkie’s privacy policy also allows text and voice conversations to be shared with affiliated companies. And under Chinese law, companies can be required to assist intelligence agencies and hand data over for national security investigations. China data policy expert Nigel Cory told a US congressional commission in April: “A Chinese firm does not need to be tasked with data collection for its overseas data to be accessible to Chinese state actors as the compulsion architecture is always on, regardless of whether it is being actively used.” MiniMax told investors it stores Chinese and overseas users’ data separately. It’s not clear whether its Chinese operations can access Talkie chats, including children’s. China has imposed strict rules governing children’s relationships with AI. Since July, providers have been prohibited from offering “virtual relatives or partners” to under-18s. Chatbots are also prohibited from encouraging emotional dependence or addiction. But Chinese companies can still offer these services to children abroad. Australia is now moving to tackle the emotional harm caused by AI companions. On 28 October, its House of Representatives passed legislation containing an amendment targeting chatbots that simulate emotional intimacy and encourage children to develop bonds with AI instead of people. The bill was debated in the Senate this week. The UK’s proposed chatbot restrictions, set to come into effect next year, would bar under-18s from services primarily offering sexual relationships and require age checks for sexually explicit features on general-purpose chatbots. But it would still leave children able to use other companion apps and become attached to their characters, as we reported in June⁠ . Apple introduced new rules on 16 November requiring developers to declare whether their apps feature virtual companions engaging users in sexual or romantic content and to give any that do a minimum 18+ rating. We asked MiniMax about Talkie’s age checks, its policies and how conversations on the app are used to train AI models. MiniMax did not respond to our questions. * Name has been changed Samaritans can be contacted 24 hours a day, 365 days a year on freephone 116 123 or by email at jo@samaritans.org .
